"AI validating AI." 🔍

That's the phrase industry analysts started using in mid-2026 to describe what's happening in recruitment.

Candidate uses AI to write their CV → Recruiter uses AI to screen it → Client uses AI to conduct the interview

At no point does a human meaningfully evaluate whether the candidate can actually do the job.

Each AI validates the previous one's output.

And somewhere along the way, the gap between what the candidate can do and what their profile says they can do stops being caught.

Recruiterflow's July 2026 industry report named AI candidate fraud "an explicit factor reshaping how RPO contracts and reporting get structured going into 2027."

CV verification is quickly becoming a core recruiter skill — not just a compliance concern.

If your AI audit can't see inside the lab, it isn't an AI audit.

It's a brochure review.

There's a big difference between checking a model and checking the system.

The model is the software. The system is everything around it: the people who train it, what 

they hide, who can speak freely about problems, and how the AI is used to make decisions that affect people.

Hiring. 
Credit.
 Safety. 
Customer decisions.

A model can look fine in a test and still be the wrong thing to put into that kind of decision.
That's why desk access matters for AI assurance.

You're not only asking: "Does the model work?" 

You're asking: "Can someone independent see the full picture?"

Anthropic said it will let outside evaluators work inside the company like staff (Amodei, "We Must Pace the Frontier").

Desks. Badges. 

Same kind of tools as the internal risk team. Right to publish findings without the lab rewriting them.

Altman told Fortune OpenAI will do the same.

If you buy AI assurance, make this your floor:

✅ Put real access in the SOW before kickoff 

✅ Lock the right to publish (write the redaction rules down)
 
✅ Check how the AI is built and run, not only the finished model 

✅ Name the AI governance owner who acts on the report 

✅ Say no to deck-only "assurance"

Responsible AI without evidence is theatre. Your contracts can raise the bar before the law does.

What access terms are in your next AI audit SOW?

💡 A recent article from Bloomberg Law examines how the growing AI race among major law firms is beginning to affect the lateral hiring market. While firms are investing heavily in AI tools and promoting their technological capabilities, the article suggests that lawyers are unlikely to move firms simply because one firm has access to a more advanced AI platform. Instead, AI is becoming an indicator of a firm's broader strategy, leadership and willingness to adapt to changes in the legal industry.

The article explains that sophisticated lateral candidates are increasingly interested in how AI is actually being integrated into legal practice. They want to know whether AI is being used meaningfully in areas such as legal research, drafting, knowledge management and client service, whether lawyers are receiving adequate training, and whether the technology is producing tangible benefits for clients. Firms that cannot demonstrate practical implementation risk appearing as though their AI investments are primarily for marketing rather than genuine transformation.

A key point is that AI should be viewed as a strategic and organisational issue rather than simply a technology purchase. The article highlights areas such as international trade, national security, export controls and government contracts, where AI can help lawyers process large volumes of rapidly changing information and identify relevant issues more efficiently. This could allow lawyers to spend less time on routine, mechanical tasks and more time providing the strategic judgment and expertise that clients value.

Ultimately, the article argues that AI is becoming a signal of how well a law firm is positioned for the future. Firms that successfully integrate AI into their workflows, training, client service and overall business strategy may gain an advantage in attracting both clients and talented lawyers. As basic AI tools become increasingly widespread, the real differentiator may not be which technology a firm has purchased, but whether the firm has a clear vision for how AI will fundamentally change the way its lawyers work and deliver value.

🤖 Every EOR provider is launching an AI agent this year. G-P has Gia. Deel has its AI suite. The pitches all sound identical.

Here's what the data actually says about AI in HR — and why "AI vs human" is the wrong framing for anyone hiring in Southeast Asia 👇

---

📊 The adoption numbers are real:

🔸 48% of large enterprises already run agentic AI in HR (ADP)
🔸 CHROs project 327% growth in AI agent adoption by 2027
🔸 Gartner: 33% of enterprise software will include agentic AI by 2028 — up from under 1% in 2024

The direction is clear. AI is becoming the default layer of HR operations — contracts, payroll validation, onboarding workflows, compliance checks.

---

⚠️ But here's the part nobody puts in the pitch deck:

Gartner also predicts 40%+ of agentic AI projects will be CANCELED by end of 2027 — inadequate governance, unclear value, rising costs. And 79% of IT leaders say AI agents create new security challenges.

AI-generated contracts are only as good as the regulatory data behind them. An AI agent that drafts a Vietnamese employment contract in 90 seconds is worthless if it misses a Tet bonus clause that local courts actually enforce.

---

🧭 So what does this mean for EOR buyers in SEA?

The question was never "AI or humans." It's "which provider combines both?"

👉 AI handles the 80%: contract generation, document verification, payroll calculations, deadline tracking. This should take minutes, not days.

👉 Local experts handle the 20% that actually creates risk: regulatory interpretation, edge cases, cultural judgment, and the moment something goes wrong and a real person needs to own the fix.

The five SEA markets don't share a rulebook. Indonesia's BPJS, Vietnam's social insurance, the Philippines' 13th month pay, Malaysia's EPF — no single AI model navigates all of them perfectly. The providers who pretend it does are selling you their gaps.

---

🔸 At Glints, we've been pragmatic about this: AI speeds up our workflows across all 5 SEA markets, and our local compliance teams in each country review what matters. Speed from machines. Judgment from people who've operated in these markets for years.

That combination — not AI alone — is what lets a client's first hire in a new market start in days instead of quarters.

Most non-technical founders lose control of their AI product before the first invoice is even cleared.

If you are hiring an outside agency or contractor, do not sign on scope alone.

Here are 4 clauses missing from 90% of AI dev proposals:

1.⁠ ⁠Full Prompt & Schema Repository Ownership
•⁠ ⁠Most agencies store prompts and schemas inside third-party SaaS dashboards or agency tools.
•⁠ ⁠If you part ways, you lose the core instructions of your application.
•⁠ ⁠Require prompts, system instructions, and structured schemas committed directly to your company Git repo before milestone sign-off.

2.⁠ ⁠Eval Dataset & Regression Suite Delivery
•⁠ ⁠Clean staging demos frequently fail when messy data hits production.
•⁠ ⁠Require the agency to deliver a 50+ item test dataset of edge cases and ground truths.
•⁠ ⁠Tie the final milestone payout to measuring accuracy against this test suite.

3.⁠ ⁠Isolated API Billing & Account Provisioning
•⁠ ⁠Never route production traffic through agency proxy keys or marked-up accounts.
•⁠ ⁠An issue with an external developer account can disrupt your entire service.
•⁠ ⁠All LLM API keys must run directly through your own OpenAI, Anthropic, or AWS accounts from day one.

4.⁠ ⁠Deterministic Fallback & Latency SLA
•⁠ ⁠AI models fail unpredictably with timeouts, malformed JSON, and hallucinations.
•⁠ ⁠Your contract requires deterministic fallback handling when models fail.
•⁠ ⁠Set clear token and cost bounds per user action, alongside strict latency requirements.

I didn't learn freight pricing from a manager. I learned it from a spreadsheet I built to get out of the work.

Nowadays, AI would have done it in seconds, and I wouldn't have learned a thing.

Every quotation I did meant pulling together routes, transit times, and costs from a pile of documents. Same files, same answers, over and over. (That was annoying AF.)

So I built the thing that did it for me. It cut 80 or 90% of the lookup time.
That beautiful spreadsheet made me faster. And for a short while I felt like a genius 😅.

Building it made me good, though. To create it, I had to go through all of it myself. The routes. The exceptions. The numbers that actually mattered.

A lot of it stuck. I knew everything in that sheet by heart.

USC economist Miao Ben Zhang writes about this in a paper called The Broken Job Ladder. It argues that junior work always produced two things.

1️⃣ The company got the work.
2️⃣ The junior employee got the reps.

The contract got reviewed while someone learned what to look for. The research got done while someone learned which source to trust. The PowerPoint got built while someone learned what their boss actually wanted.

Nobody had to pay for getting those reps. It was simply part of the job and came free with the work that you produced. 

Now though, AI gives us the first one without the second.

That's useful. I use it every day.

According to Stanford's Digital Economy Lab's recently updated research, for workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed jobs, employment is running about 19% below where you'd expect. Mostly from hiring fewer people, not firing more.

What it means is that we're pulling rungs out of the ladder.

I call it the apprenticeship severance. Where the work and the education came from the same task that your boss gave you.  

Now they don't. 

If you still want someone to learn, you have to do it on purpose.

The junior role you cut this year is the senior hire you can't find in five.

What work made you good at what you do?

Read more about this in this week's edition.

🧠 What Should a Business Owner Know?

As I continue learning about business ownership and investment, I have been asking myself:

What knowledge does a business owner really need?

I believe a business owner doesn't need to be an expert in everything. But they need enough knowledge to **understand the bigger picture, ask the right questions, identify risks and opportunities, and make better decisions.**

💼 Core Business Knowledge

A business owner should understand:

💰 Finance & Accounting — financial statements, cash flow, profit, costs, budgeting and investment.

📣 Marketing & Sales — customers, pricing, branding, competition and customer needs.

⚙️ Operations — processes, suppliers, inventory, quality and efficiency.

👥 People & Leadership — hiring, training, delegation, communication and team culture.

⚖️ Law & Governance — tax, contracts, regulations, compliance and business risks.

💻 Technology — digital tools, AI, automation, data and cybersecurity.

🌍 Look Beyond the Business

A business does not operate in isolation.

We also need to understand:

👥 Society — demographics, income, lifestyle, consumer behavior and social trends.

📊 Economy — GDP, inflation, interest rates, exchange rates, employment and purchasing power.

🏪 Industry — market demand, competitors, pricing, supply and new technologies.

🌏 Global Environment — trade, supply chains, foreign investment, commodity prices and geopolitical risks.

🔎 Where Should We Get Information?

I would use three levels:

🥇 Primary Sources — government agencies, NBC, official statistics, company annual reports, audited financial statements, World Bank, IMF, ADB, etc.

🥈 Professional Analysis — industry reports, research, academic studies and expert analysis.

🥉 News & Social Media — useful for discovering what is happening, but important information should be verified through the original source.

My preferred process is:

See → Find the Source → Verify → Analyze → Decide

🧭 Business Owner Thinking

I am learning that these areas are connected:

Society → Economy → Market → Customer → Competition → Strategy → Finance → Operations → Risk → Decision

Therefore, becoming a business owner is not only about having a business idea.

It is about **preparing step by step to understand the environment, create value, manage risks and make responsible decisions.**

I am still learning and would be grateful to hear from experienced business owners, investors and professionals who are willing to **challenge my thinking and share what I may be missing.**

Learn → Research → Verify → Analyze → Prepare → Decide → Grow. 🌱

One of the biggest challenges businesses face today isn't simply finding people. It's finding the right people at the right time.

Everyone is talking about business growth, expansion, digitalisation and AI.

But behind every growth plan is one important question:
Do we have the people to execute it?

Singapore ended 2025 with 77,700 job vacancies, with vacancies continuing to exceed the number of unemployed persons. At the same time, employers are increasingly placing greater emphasis on skills and relevant experience, particularly for specialised roles.

The reality for many businesses can look like:
• Positions staying open for longer
• Hiring managers spending more time screening CVs
• Difficulty finding specialised talent
• Candidates receiving multiple opportunities
• Increasing salary expectations
• Pressure on existing teams to take on additional workload
• The cost of making the wrong hire

And when a critical position remains vacant, the impact can go beyond recruitment.
Projects can be delayed.
Teams can become stretched.
Business opportunities can be missed.

This is why recruitment today needs to be more than simply filling vacancies.

It can be about understanding the business requirement, knowing the talent market, identifying where relevant talent sits and determining the right hiring approach for each situation.

Whether that means permanent recruitment, targeted headhunting, executive search, contract or temporary staffing, the solution should depend on what the business actually needs.

The question businesses should be asking isn't only:
“How do we fill this position?”

But:
“How do we build the workforce we need to support our business goals?”
Because ultimately, recruitment isn't just an HR function.
It is part of business strategy.

Day 88: Is Hiring Enough When Talent Is Hard to Find?

Sometimes, the problem is not finding candidates. It is finding candidates with the exact skills the business needs. I came across a recent ETHRWorld article about the growing talent shortage in the pharmaceutical industry, and one point stood out to me.

More than 80% of pharma companies reported shortages in specialised areas such as clinical research, regulatory sciences, computational biology, gene editing and AI-driven drug discovery. But the bigger challenge is not simply that there are fewer people available.

It is that companies increasingly need people who bring a combination of skills. For example, someone who understands both pharma and data science, or regulatory work and AI governance, can be much harder to find than someone with expertise in just one area.

And this creates a very practical question for HR: What do you do when the talent you need is simply not available in the market? The answer cannot always be “keep hiring until we find the perfect candidate.”

Companies mentioned in the article are trying different approaches:
• Hiring people with adjacent skills and developing them internally.
• Moving employees across functions through job rotations.
• Creating internal talent marketplaces.
• Using fractional or contract specialists for niche requirements.
• Building talent pipelines through universities and academic institutions.

This made me think about recruitment differently. Sometimes the solution to a hiring problem is not better sourcing. It may be better talent development. If the market doesn't have enough people with the exact skills a company needs, organisations may have to start asking that "Can we build some of this talent ourselves?”

For HR, that means recruitment and learning & development cannot always work separately. Hiring brings talent in. Learning helps build the talent we cannot find.

Learning this from Parth Verma Sir as a part of my #100DaysWithTVS challenge.

Fastcode AI offers a fixed-price “Research as a Service” that delivers a conference-ready manuscript for $100 000 within three to four months. The model promises co-authorship on an accepted paper, turning a client-defined AI problem into a peer-reviewed record without the overhead of building an internal research team.

The company’s website details a five-stage workflow: problem definition, scoping, execution, submission, and review response. All engagements are capped at a single $100 k payment and a 3–4 month window calibrated to typical conference deadlines. The founder, Arjun Jain, showcases a “track record” of nine recent works, five of which are published (WACV 2026, WACV 2023, ICCV 2021, AAAI 2021, CVPR 2020). Those five appeared before Fastcode AI existed and list only Jain’s prior institutional affiliations, never the firm itself. Four additional entries are marked “in review” (AAAI 2027, ICLR 2027, ACL 2027, NeurIPS 2026) but are not searchable on arXiv or OpenAlex, so their status remains unverified.

If the service delivers a paper that passes peer review, the client gains a venue-level credibility signal at predictable cost and timeline—a tempting alternative to hiring a research team or negotiating university collaborations. At the same time, the lack of a publication guarantee, the absence of open-source artifacts, and the opacity around the actual team size raise questions about reproducibility and the long-term value of such commodified research.

The offering also highlights a broader shift toward treating academic output as a billable deliverable, which could pressure conference review processes and blur the line between independent scholarship and client-driven engineering. Stakeholders will need to monitor how often these contracts translate into truly novel contributions versus repackaged existing work.

FastCode AI positions the model as the only option that combines a fixed fee, a short, defined submission window, and a built-in resubmission step, but the public record currently provides no concrete examples of a client-co-authored, accepted manuscript.

Changing your mind is cheap. Building the capability the new view demands is the expensive part, and Yasmin was the one in the room actually building it.

She had a hiring plan in front of her and she hated it. It was a sensible plan. It listed the gaps her function had today and proposed people to fill them today. A senior buyer here, an analyst there, a contract manager to clear the backlog. Every line was justifiable. The whole thing was a trap.

The myth is that you hire to close today's capability gaps. The reality is that staffing for the function you have guarantees you'll never have the one you need. You hire for the work that's visible, and the work that matters is arriving from a direction the org chart doesn't face.

So she tore it up and asked a different question. Not what is broken now, but what will this function need to be good at by 2028, and who do I hire today who can grow into that. What surfaced was less a checklist than a compass.

Four capabilities surfaced, none of them a job title. 
1. People who can decide under uncertainty, not just analyze toward certainty, because the function was thick with analysts and thin with deciders.
2. People who can author meaning into data, define a category, hold a taxonomy, the authorship she'd built her division on.
3. People fluent enough in AI to know what to trust it with and, more importantly, what not to, where the judgment stays human. And, 
4. People who can hold a supplier relationship as a long game, warm for a year before it pays, because no model does that and it remains the quiet heart of the work.

None of those was a role she could post. They were capabilities, and capabilities cut across the neat boxes of a job description. That was the point. The boxes were built for the function she had. The capabilities were for the function she would need.

Every CPO has felt this and flinched. You're training people for a job that is changing faster than they can learn it. The role moves underneath them while they're still reading the manual.

Yasmin's answer was not to predict the role precisely. Nobody can. It was to hire for adaptability over fit, judgment over throughput, and to accept that some of these people would be slightly wrong for today in exchange for being right for the thing she could see coming.

Capabilities are inputs. The question is what they add up to when a transformation actually works.

Yasmin is fictional. Any resemblance to actual companies is coincidental.

Technical controls cannot resolve every business decision.

Anthropic describes AI safety as interdisciplinary, bringing researchers, engineers, policy experts and operators into the same process.

For enterprise automation, that is more than a hiring strategy.

It is a design principle.

Workflows do not fail only when AI accesses the wrong system.

They also fail when valid business rules point towards different actions.

A contract clause may match the legal template but exceed the approved commercial risk.

An invoice may match the PO and GRN while containing bank details changed after vendor approval.

Both can pass their technical checks.

Neither should proceed automatically.

When we design agentic workflows at Mavdero, we map decision rights before automating tasks:

What may the agent decide?
What evidence must support the decision?
Which exception requires human approval?
Who owns that exception?
How will the decision be reconstructed later?

Those answers become policy checks, approval gates, escalation paths and audit records.

The agent can process the document, identify the conflict and prepare the next action.

It should not invent authority when the rules stop.

Is your AI governed well enough to know when not to decide?
